sources.entry: Teach Yourself Computer Science: an opinionated set of the best CS resources.

summary.title: Teach Yourself Computer Science
summary.one_liner: A curated, opinionated path through nine core computer science subjects, with a recommended book and video course for each, aimed at self-taught engineers and bootcamp grads.
keywords: structure and interpretation of computer programs
what should a software engineer learn about computer science
takeaways: Study nine core CS subjects (programming, architecture, algorithms, math, operating systems, networking, databases, languages and compilers, distributed systems), roughly 100-200 hours each.
For each subject, the guide names one recommended book and one video course, such as SICP with Brian Harvey's CS 61A lectures and CS:APP for architecture.
If time is limited, focus on Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective and Designing Data-Intensive Applications.
Learn CS before tools: computer architecture before operating systems or databases, and networking and OS before distributed systems.
Electives suggested: AI (Berkeley intro AI, Russell and Norvig), machine learning (Andrew Ng's Coursera course), and computer graphics (Berkeley CS 184).
summary.summary: This guide argues that self-taught engineers should learn computer science fundamentals and lays out nine subjects in a suggested order. For each subject it explains why it matters and recommends a primary textbook and a video lecture series, with notes on alternatives and practice (such as Leetcode problems, exercism, xv6, and Wireshark labs). It also covers prerequisites, how the topics overlap, electives, and why learning specific languages or tools matters less than underlying concepts.
